title: Snowflake ID Generator
description: Build a unique, time-ordered id generator from a timestamp, a worker id and a per-millisecond sequence.
statement:
Build `SnowflakeGenerator(worker_id, clock, wait, epoch=0)`, which hands out unique, increasing 64-bit-style ids without talking to any other machine. `clock()` returns the current time in whole milliseconds. `wait()` takes no arguments and returns after about a millisecond has passed (in the tests it advances the fake clock by exactly 1 ms, and nothing else does).

`next_id()` reads `now = clock()` and returns `((now - epoch) << 22) | (worker_id << 12) | sequence`:

- The first id, and the first id of every new millisecond, uses `sequence = 0`. Another id in the same millisecond as the last one uses the last sequence + 1.
- The sequence has 12 bits (0 to 4095). When a millisecond already has 4096 ids, call `wait()` until `clock()` reports a later millisecond, and use that one.
- If `clock()` is earlier than the millisecond of the last id, raise `ClockMovedBackwards`. That call changes nothing, so the generator works again once the clock catches up.
- `worker_id` must be 0 to 1023, otherwise the constructor raises `ValueError`.

**Example**

```python
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(3, clock, wait, epoch=1000)   # clock() reads 1005
gen.next_id()   # 20983808  = (5 << 22) | (3 << 12) | 0
gen.next_id()   # 20983809  same millisecond, sequence 1
# the clock moves to 1006
gen.next_id()   # 25178112  = (6 << 22) | (3 << 12) | 0
```

tests.name: the example: the sequence counts up inside a millisecond and restarts in the next
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(1005)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(3, clock, clock.wait, epoch=1000)
assert gen.next_id() == 20983808
assert gen.next_id() == 20983809
clock.set(1006)
assert gen.next_id() == 25178112

tests.name: five ids in one millisecond differ only in the sequence, and wait() is not called
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(1005)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(3, clock, clock.wait, epoch=1000)
ids = [gen.next_id() for _ in range(5)]
assert ids == [(5 << 22) | (3 << 12) | sequence for sequence in range(5)]
assert clock.waits == 0, f"wait() was called {clock.waits} time(s) although no millisecond was full"

tests.name: the very first id may be issued at the epoch itself (sequence 0, not 1)
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(500)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(1, clock, clock.wait, epoch=500)
assert gen.next_id() == 1 << 12
assert gen.next_id() == (1 << 12) | 1
default = FakeClock(0)
assert SnowflakeGenerator(0, default, default.wait).next_id() == 0, "epoch defaults to 0"

tests.name: real-world timestamps: milliseconds since 1970 with a custom epoch, and time jumping ahead
tests.code:
epoch = 1_735_689_600_000
clock = FakeClock(epoch + 123_456_789)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(513, clock, clock.wait, epoch=epoch)
assert gen.next_id() == (123_456_789 << 22) | (513 << 12)
clock.set(epoch + 123_456_792)
assert gen.next_id() == (123_456_792 << 22) | (513 << 12)

tests.name: two workers asking in the same millisecond never get the same id
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(2000)
a = SnowflakeGenerator(1, clock, clock.wait, epoch=1000)
b = SnowflakeGenerator(2, clock, clock.wait, epoch=1000)
ids_a = [a.next_id() for _ in range(5)]
ids_b = [b.next_id() for _ in range(5)]
assert set(ids_a).isdisjoint(ids_b), f"workers 1 and 2 produced the same id: {sorted(set(ids_a) & set(ids_b))}"
assert ids_b[0] - ids_a[0] == 1 << 12, "the worker id sits in bits 12 to 21, just above the sequence"

tests.name: a millisecond holds 4096 ids (sequence 0 to 4095); if the clock moved on by itself nothing waits
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(5000)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(1023, clock, clock.wait)
ids = [gen.next_id() for _ in range(4096)]
assert ids[0] == (5000 << 22) | (1023 << 12) | 0
assert ids[-1] == (5000 << 22) | (1023 << 12) | 4095
assert clock.waits == 0
clock.set(5001)
assert gen.next_id() == (5001 << 22) | (1023 << 12) | 0
assert clock.waits == 0, "the clock had already moved to the next millisecond, so there is nothing to wait for"

tests.name: the 4097th id in a millisecond waits for the next millisecond and restarts the sequence at 0
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(5000)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(7, clock, clock.wait)
for _ in range(4096):
    gen.next_id()
assert gen.next_id() == (5001 << 22) | (7 << 12) | 0
assert clock.waits == 1, f"expected one call to wait(), got {clock.waits}"
assert gen.next_id() == (5001 << 22) | (7 << 12) | 1

tests.name: a burst of 9000 ids in a frozen clock: strictly increasing, using two extra milliseconds
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(10_000)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(7, clock, clock.wait)
ids = [gen.next_id() for _ in range(9000)]
assert all(earlier < later for earlier, later in zip(ids, ids[1:])), "ids must be strictly increasing"
assert clock.waits == 2, f"9000 ids need 3 milliseconds (4096 per millisecond), so 2 waits; wait() was called {clock.waits} times"
assert ids[-1] == (10_002 << 22) | (7 << 12) | 807

tests.name: a clock that goes backwards raises ClockMovedBackwards and the failed call changes nothing
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(2000)
gen = SnowflakeGenerator(0, clock, clock.wait)
first = gen.next_id()
clock.set(1999)
assert raises(ClockMovedBackwards, gen.next_id)
clock.set(2000)
assert gen.next_id() == first + 1, "the refused call must not use up or reset the sequence"
clock.set(2001)
assert gen.next_id() == 2001 << 22

tests.name: worker ids must fit in 10 bits: 0 to 1023
tests.code:
clock = FakeClock(0)
assert raises(ValueError, SnowflakeGenerator, 1024, clock, clock.wait)
assert raises(ValueError, SnowflakeGenerator, -1, clock, clock.wait)
assert SnowflakeGenerator(1023, clock, clock.wait).next_id() == 1023 << 12

hints: An id is three numbers glued into one integer. Which operation moves a number left by a fixed number of bits so the three fields do not overlap? And what must the generator remember between calls to know whether this is a new millisecond?

Remember the millisecond of the last id and its sequence. Same millisecond: sequence + 1. Later millisecond: sequence 0. When sequence + 1 would be 4096 the millisecond is full: call `wait()` until `clock()` has moved past it.
Start "the last millisecond" as `None`, not as 0 or the epoch, or the very first id at the epoch looks like a repeat. Check for a backwards clock before you change any state.
solution:
WORKER_BITS = 10
SEQUENCE_BITS = 12
MAX_WORKER_ID = (1 << WORKER_BITS) - 1
MAX_SEQUENCE = (1 << SEQUENCE_BITS) - 1


class ClockMovedBackwards(Exception):
    """clock() reported a time earlier than the millisecond of the last id."""


class SnowflakeGenerator:
    def __init__(self, worker_id, clock, wait, epoch=0):
        if not 0 <= worker_id <= MAX_WORKER_ID:
            raise ValueError(f"worker_id must be between 0 and {MAX_WORKER_ID}, got {worker_id}")
        self._worker_id = worker_id
        self._clock = clock
        self._wait = wait
        self._epoch = epoch
        self._last_ms = None   # millisecond of the last id; None until the first one (0 would clash with an epoch-time id)
        self._sequence = 0

    def next_id(self):
        now = self._clock()
        if self._last_ms is not None and now < self._last_ms:
            raise ClockMovedBackwards(f"clock went back {self._last_ms - now} ms; refusing to issue an id")
        if now == self._last_ms:
            sequence = self._sequence + 1
            if sequence > MAX_SEQUENCE:            # this millisecond is full: wait for the next one
                while now <= self._last_ms:
                    self._wait()
                    now = self._clock()
                sequence = 0
        else:
            sequence = 0
        self._last_ms, self._sequence = now, sequence
        return ((now - self._epoch) << (WORKER_BITS + SEQUENCE_BITS)) | (self._worker_id << SEQUENCE_BITS) | sequence
explanation:
**The idea.** An id is three fields packed into one integer: the time since a custom epoch in the high bits, then the worker id, then a sequence number in the low bits. Because time is in the high bits, ids sort by creation time. Because each worker has its own bits, two workers can never collide. Because the sequence counts the ids inside one millisecond, one worker never repeats itself either. After each worker has been given its number, no coordination is needed.

**The state is two numbers:** the millisecond of the last id and its sequence. Same millisecond: sequence + 1. Later millisecond: sequence 0. If sequence + 1 would be 4096 the millisecond is full, so wait for the clock to move on and start again at 0. Start with "no previous millisecond" (`None`), not `0`, or an id issued exactly at the epoch looks like a repeat.

**A clock that goes backwards** (an NTP correction, a VM resumed from a pause) would issue an id smaller than one already handed out, possibly a duplicate. Refusing is the safe choice. Check it before you change any state, so a refused call leaves nothing behind.

**Complexity.** O(1) per id, apart from the wait. Follow-up: what happens when a worker restarts and forgets `_last_ms`? (Persist it, or wait out the largest clock skew you tolerate before issuing.)
